canonical_statement: The review aimed to evaluate VTE chemoprophylaxis dosing regimens in obese trauma and surgical patients for efficacy and safety using VTE incidence, anti-factor Xa attainment, and bleeding events.
PICO 1 asked whether weight-adjusted chemoprophylaxis is superior to alternate regimens in obese trauma and surgery patients for VTE incidence, bleeding, or therapeutic anti-factor Xa attainment.

PICO 2 asked whether high fixed-dose chemoprophylaxis is superior to standard fixed-dose regimens in obese trauma and surgery patients for VTE incidence, bleeding, or therapeutic anti-factor Xa attainment.
The systematic review was conducted according to PRISMA guidance.
Seven databases were searched for publications from January 2000 through April 2019: PubMed, EMBASE, GoogleScholar, JAMA Network, CINAHL, Cochrane, and SAGE Journals.
Search terms included combinations of VTE prophylaxis, pulmonary embolism, DVT, enoxaparin, obesity, bariatric, trauma, and surgery.
Reference lists of retrieved studies were examined to identify additional eligible studies.
The search was restricted to English-language studies, and the final search was performed on April 28, 2019.
Eligible studies evaluated pharmacologic VTE prevention in obese trauma or surgery patients, with high-risk hospitalized patients such as ICU patients also eligible.

population.label: Obese trauma, surgical, or high-risk hospitalized patients

canonical_statement: The review imposed no restrictions on pharmacologic agent, sample size, patient age, or follow-up duration because of limited available evidence.

population.label: Candidate studies of pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis in obesity

canonical_statement: Outpatient studies were excluded to preserve greater homogeneity in VTE risk.

population.label: Outpatient participants

canonical_statement: Studies were excluded when the exact chemoprophylaxis dose or regimen and either VTE incidence or anti-factor Xa outcomes were not reported.

population.label: Candidate studies lacking required regimen or outcome detail
exclusion_criteria: No exact dose/regimen or no VTE/anti-Xa outcome

canonical_statement: Systematic reviews, meta-analyses, case series, case reports, literature reviews, surveys, short notes, and letters were excluded.

population.label: Non-original or low-detail publication types

canonical_statement: Two reviewers conducted the literature search, article screening, and full-text data extraction, and two authors resolved inclusion or exclusion questions.

Extracted study fields included citation, year, location, center, design, sample size, population, age, BMI, weight, prophylaxis agent, protocol, dose regimen, target anti-factor Xa, limitations, and outcomes.
Primary review outcomes were VTE chemoprophylaxis regimen, VTE incidence, anti-factor Xa goal, and bleeding events.

outcome.definition: Chemoprophylaxis regimen, VTE incidence, anti-factor Xa goal, and bleeding events

canonical_statement: Secondary outcomes were BMI, goal anti-factor Xa, surgical procedures, and concomitant VTE risk factors.

outcome.definition: BMI, goal anti-factor Xa, surgical procedures, and concomitant VTE risk factors

canonical_statement: Risk of bias in randomized controlled trials was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Assessment Tool.
Evidence quality was assessed using GRADE, incorporating inconsistency, imprecision, indirectness, and other limitations.
The Caprini risk assessment model was used to assess consistency of patient risk status across included studies.
The search identified 5,083 citations before screening.

population.label: Citations identified in database and reference searching

canonical_statement: After duplicate removal and title screening, 206 citations remained.

population.label: Records after duplicates and irrelevant titles were removed

canonical_statement: Seventy-three records were excluded on abstract review or because full text could not be obtained, leaving 133 full-text articles assessed for eligibility.

population.label: Full-text eligibility stage

canonical_statement: Forty-five studies comprising 27,717 patients met inclusion criteria.

population.label: Participants across 45 included studies

canonical_statement: Four of the 45 included studies were randomized controlled trials.

population.label: Included randomized controlled trials

canonical_statement: Six weight-based studies included 458 patients.

population.label: Participants in weight-based dosing studies

canonical_statement: Four weight-stratified studies included 1,497 patients.

population.label: Participants in weight-stratified dosing studies

canonical_statement: Five BMI-stratified studies included 732 patients.

population.label: Participants in BMI-stratified dosing studies

canonical_statement: Two studies evaluating continuous heparin infusion included 841 patients.

population.label: Participants in continuous heparin infusion studies

canonical_statement: Twenty-nine fixed-dose studies included 24,274 patients.

population.label: Participants in fixed-dose prophylaxis studies

canonical_statement: One included study contributed to both weight-based and BMI-stratified analyses but was not counted twice in the overall patient total.
Among the four randomized trials, two were judged to have fair risk of bias and two low risk of bias.
The overall quality of evidence for the dosing regimens was rated low.
Evidence quality for BMI-stratified dosing and continuous infusion was rated very low.
Subgroup analyses were not performed because the evidence base lacked sufficient high-quality data.
Across included studies, weight-based regimens more often produced anti-factor Xa values in the target range.
Fixed-dose regimens commonly produced subtherapeutic anti-factor Xa values.
The review found a negative relationship between patient weight and anti-factor Xa concentration.
Bleeding events were observed predominantly when anti-factor Xa values were therapeutic or subtherapeutic rather than clearly supratherapeutic.
The review found no meaningful association between VTE incidence and bleeding events across the analyzed studies.
Most included studies used a prophylactic anti-factor Xa target range of approximately 0.2 to 0.6 IU/mL.

outcome.definition: Target range used in most included studies was approximately 0.2–0.6 IU/mL

canonical_statement: All six weight-based enoxaparin studies used anti-factor Xa target attainment as the primary outcome.
Across the weight-based studies, 277 patients received enoxaparin 0.5 mg/kg twice daily and 96 patients received 0.5 mg/kg once daily.

canonical_statement: Twenty-nine studies evaluated fixed-dose prophylaxis; agents represented included enoxaparin, unfractionated heparin, nadroparin, parnaparin, dalteparin, and fondaparinux.
Among fixed-dose studies, 12 evaluated enoxaparin 40 mg twice daily, seven evaluated 40 mg once daily, two evaluated 60 mg once daily, and one evaluated 60 mg twice daily.
A cohort comparing enoxaparin 40 mg twice daily with unfractionated heparin 5,000 units three times daily found no significant difference in VTE incidence.

In the same enoxaparin-versus-heparin cohort, blood transfusion occurred in 14 enoxaparin patients (5.9%) versus three heparin patients (1.3%), with p=0.011; four enoxaparin patients required reoperation for bleeding.

canonical_statement: For PICO 1, the authors concluded that weight-based regimens may be superior to BMI-stratified and standard fixed-dose regimens for achieving target anti-factor Xa in obese trauma and surgical patients.
For PICO 1, the authors also concluded that weight-stratified regimens may be superior to standard fixed-dose regimens for anti-factor Xa target attainment.
The PICO 1 recommendation was graded Weak (2B).
For PICO 2, the authors concluded that high fixed-dose regimens increase bleeding without a corresponding reduction in VTE compared with standard fixed-dose regimens.
The PICO 2 recommendation was graded Weak (2B).
The authors noted that many studies achieved target anti-factor Xa concentrations, but few demonstrated a reduction in VTE formation.
The authors found no obvious correlation between anti-factor Xa concentration and VTE incidence in obese trauma and surgery patients.
The authors concluded that weight-adjusted regimens improved anti-factor Xa target attainment but were not associated with fewer VTE events.
With the exception of the Scholten study, the authors concluded that high fixed-dose enoxaparin was associated with more bleeding without a corresponding decrease in VTE.
The discussion stated that enoxaparin achieves target anti-factor Xa more successfully than unfractionated heparin but is associated with more bleeding in the reviewed obese populations.
The authors acknowledged high risk of bias in many included studies.
Only four randomized trials were identified, and only three of those assessed VTE incidence as a primary outcome.
Outcome follow-up was inconsistent across studies, ranging from in-hospital reporting to 30-day or 90-day follow-up, and some studies had loss to follow-up.
Most included studies had small samples and were not powered to draw conclusions about VTE incidence.
Most studies emphasized anti-factor Xa target attainment even though the relationship between anti-factor Xa and clinical VTE occurrence has not been established.
The prophylactic anti-factor Xa target was not uniformly defined across studies, limiting comparability.
Some dosing schemes contained BMI or weight gaps between groups, making the regimens difficult to reproduce.
Some studies did not report bleeding events or did not distinguish major from minor bleeding, preventing robust comparative safety assessment.
The evidence base was dominated by bariatric surgery and, to a lesser extent, cesarean populations, limiting direct generalizability to other obese surgical and trauma populations.
The authors stated that further investigation is needed before formal practice-changing recommendations can be made because overall risk of bias is high and evidence quality is low.
Future studies were advised to report both weight and BMI because their relative value for predicting thrombotic and bleeding outcomes remains uncertain.
The authors recommended further study of extended postdischarge chemoprophylaxis in obese postoperative patients.
Future studies were advised to distinguish major from minor bleeding complications.
The authors recommended that future prospective trials use VTE incidence rather than anti-factor Xa target attainment as a primary outcome.
Future investigations were advised to include obese pediatric and adolescent patients.
The final conclusion was that weight-based and high fixed-dose regimens reached target anti-factor Xa more often than standard fixed-dose regimens but did not reduce VTE.
The final conclusion was that high fixed-dose prophylaxis was associated with increased bleeding complications.
The authors called for large multicenter randomized trials in obese trauma and surgical patients to determine the optimal VTE chemoprophylaxis dosing strategy.
The authors reported no funding.
The authors declared no conflicts of interest.
